contents.title: A Single-Writer SQLite Core
contents.summary: Why one backend owns all business data and a single SQLite connection keeps write ordering trivial.
contents.body:
# A Single-Writer SQLite Core

Every read and write flows through one process, which lets SQLite operate as a serialized single-writer store.

## Why one writer

When only one connection writes, transactions are trivially serializable without busy retries.

## What the admin gets

A deterministic content store, cheap backups, and no distributed-cache invalidation between services.

contents.title: Cache Coherence by ID
contents.summary: Invalidating public caches by content identifier instead of by whole-list keys.
contents.body:
# Cache Coherence by ID

A content row changes rarely, but aggregate lists change whenever any row does.

## Key by identifier

The public detail is cached by slug; any mutation drops the matching key.

## Derived fields stay at the core

Excerpts and reading minutes are derived at write time so the cache never holds a stale projection.

contents.title: A Public Relay Gateway
contents.summary: A small public gateway for experiments and personal infrastructure.
contents.body:
# A Public Relay Gateway

The relay exposes a handful of endpoints so side projects can share one entry point.

## What it forwards

Requests pass through rate limiting and presence tracking before reaching a backend.

## Why keep it public

Experiments need a stable URL that does not change when the underlying service moves.

contents.title: OpenList, a Calm Index
contents.summary: A quiet place to keep files, links, and things worth holding close.
contents.body:
# OpenList, a Calm Index

OpenList is a deliberate counterweight to feeds that demand attention.

## Gather instead of stream

Items are collected and organized by hand rather than pushed by an algorithm.

## What calm means here

Fewer choices per view, and no unread badge.

contents.title: Compile-Time Schema Guards
contents.summary: Refusing to open a database whose schema the binary does not know.
contents.body:
# Compile-Time Schema Guards

The migration list is embedded into the binary at build time.

## A newer database refuses to open

If the on-disk schema version exceeds what the binary knows, the process stops instead of degrading.

## Embedded migrations

There is exactly one source of truth for the schema, versioned and immutable.

contents.title: Rate Limiting as a Conversation
contents.summary: Throttling, presence, and backpressure read as a dialogue with the visitor.
contents.body:
# Rate Limiting as a Conversation

Limits are most useful when they read as guidance rather than a wall.

## Buckets by origin

Trusted proxies supply a cleaned client address to bucket requests.

## Backpressure

A paced failure tells the client to slow down without losing trust.

contents.title: Validation at the Boundary
contents.summary: Strict decoding and field checks at the HTTP edge keep the store honest.
contents.body:
# Validation at the Boundary

The HTTP handler rejects unknown fields and wrong types before a write reaches the store.

## Strict decoding

DisallowUnknownFields means a typo cannot silently drop a column.

## Derived fields are not input

Reading minutes and TOC are computed by the core, never accepted from the client.

contents.title: Observability Without a Dashboard
contents.summary: Audit events and a system status endpoint instead of a wall of graphs.
contents.body:
# Observability Without a Dashboard

An audit trail and a single health endpoint cover most of what a small service needs.

## Audit events

Every mutation is recorded with its request and trace identifiers.

## System status

One endpoint reports runtime, resources, and host in a plain shape.

contents.title: What Software Owes
contents.summary: A note on the responsibility that comes with shipping a tool.
contents.body: Most software asks for attention and rarely gives it back. A tool owes more than a feature list: it owes the clarity of not being needed. The best software becomes a habit you stop noticing.

metadata.question: What does a tool owe its users?
metadata.context: After an afternoon of quiet maintenance.

contents.title: The Cost of Defaults
contents.summary: Defaults are decisions made on your behalf.
contents.body: A default is not a neutral starting point. It is a decision made on your behalf, often to optimize for the median user you are not. Choosing the defaults deliberately is mostly work.

metadata.question: Which of my defaults are actually my choice?

contents.title: Notes on Finishing
contents.summary: Ending a project is a skill.
contents.body: Starting is generous; finishing is disciplined. The last ten percent is where a project becomes useful or remains a sketch. A good ending is smaller than the vision and sharper than the draft.

metadata.question: When is something done enough to ship?

contents.title: A Tool You Trust
contents.summary: Trust is built by predictable behavior, not promises.
contents.body: Trust in a tool is not a marketing claim. It is the accumulation of predictable behavior across many small interactions. Once trust is lost, no changelog restores it.

metadata.question: What makes a tool trustworthy?
metadata.context: Deciding whether to depend on a new library.

contents.title: Writing Is Thinking
contents.summary: Clarity of expression is clarity of thought.
contents.body: Writing is not the output of thinking; it is the process. The sentence that refuses to be written is usually an idea that refuses to be understood.

metadata.question: Do I think in order to write, or write in order to think?
metadata.context: Editing a draft at the edge of a deadline.

contents.title: Why Keep a Garden
contents.summary: A maintained space is an act of continued attention.
contents.body: A garden is not a file dump. It is a place you keep tending, pruning, and rearranging. The value is not the size of the garden but the fact that you return to it.

metadata.question: What deserves the effort of being kept?
metadata.context: A quiet morning tending the index.

contents.title: Interfaces as Constraints
contents.summary: A well-designed interface limits what can go wrong.
contents.body: An interface is not a list of things you can do. It is a set of things you cannot do wrong. The best constraint is the one that makes the correct action the easy one.

metadata.question: Where does a boundary save more than it costs?

contents.title: Pagination as a Contract
contents.summary: A paged API is a promise about ordering.
contents.body: Pagination quietly enforces an ordering promise. If the ordering is unstable, every page is a coin flip. Deterministic sorting is not a detail; it is the contract.

metadata.question: Is my ordering stable across pages?

contents.title: A Small Signal
contents.summary: Short note on when to turn an observation into a system.
contents.body: Not every observation needs a system. First decide whether it changes the way you work.
